concept.name: State-space model
concept.definition: A general time-series framework that represents observed data as noisy measurements of an unobserved state vector evolving through a transition (system) equation, separating the dynamics of the hidden process from measurement error. It subsumes ARMA models, structural time-series models, and time-varying-parameter regressions, and is estimated via the Kalman filter and maximum likelihood.
concept.intuition: Split the world into what you cannot see (the true underlying state: trend, seasonal level, drifting coefficient) and what you measure (noisy data), then let filtering theory reconstruct the hidden part.
concept.mechanics: A linear Gaussian state-space model pairs a transition equation x_t = F x_{t-1} + w_t with a measurement equation y_t = H x_t + v_t; ARMA, local-level, and local-linear-trend models are special cases with particular F and H. The Kalman filter produces one-step-ahead prediction errors whose Gaussian likelihood is maximized over the hyperparameters, and smoothing recovers the full state history.
concept.formula: x_t = F_t x_{t-1} + w_t, w_t ~ (0, Q_t); y_t = H_t x_t + v_t, v_t ~ (0, R_t).
concept.failure_modes: Noise-variance hyperparameters are often weakly identified, so different state decompositions fit equally well with different interpretations. Non-Gaussian or nonlinear models require approximate filters whose accuracy is hard to guarantee.
concept.misconceptions: That a state-space model is one specific model: it is a representation framework, and the empirical content comes entirely from the chosen state dynamics and measurement structure.
concept.example: A local-level model treats log price as a random-walk level plus observation noise; the Kalman filter estimates the level online, equivalent to an exponentially weighted average with data-driven smoothing.
